content: 1. There is a high risk of detection bias due to the loss of blinding in the studies. Additionally, significant heterogeneity was observed, with an I-squared value greater than 50%. The absolute effect was estimated as 3 more events per 1000 patients (ranging from 2 fewer to 36 more), but the certainty of evidence was rated as very low. Outcomes such as stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, cognitive impairment/dementia, and blood pressure reduction/control were not reported. 2. For the subgroup of patients with diabetic kidney disease, the total number of trials informing direct comparisons was 13. However, it is unclear which of these trials specifically examined the outcome of interest. The weight of each included study was not provided, but five of the 13 studies were judged to have an unclear risk of bias in domains such as random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessors, and selective outcome reporting. Despite this, the risk of bias was not downgraded because subgroup analyses including studies with low risk of bias showed consistent results. 3. The review did not provide I-squared values or confidence intervals for individual studies to assess heterogeneity. The review stated that a loop-specific inconsistency approach was used to assess disagreement between direct and indirect evidence, and consistency results were considered not significant when the 95% confidence intervals of inconsistency factors included zero or the relative odds ratio (RoR) included one. The RoR is defined as the difference between the odds ratio (OR) value of direct evidence and the OR value of indirect evidence. 4. Indirectness was not downgraded because a 50% drop in eGFR and doubling of serum creatinine are validated surrogate markers for end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). However, baseline risk was not reported in the network meta-analysis, and values were abstracted directly from the included studies. 5. For the subgroup of patients with diabetic kidney disease, the certainty of evidence was rated as moderate. The upper end of the 95% confidence interval crossed the threshold of 10 per 1000 patients, suggesting there may be an important harm. Outcomes such as stroke, myocardial infarction, cognitive impairment/dementia, heart failure, and blood pressure reduction/control were not reported. 6. The total number of trials informing direct comparisons for diabetic kidney disease was three. The review did not provide I-squared values or confidence intervals for individual studies to assess heterogeneity. The review stated that a loop-specific inconsistency approach was used, and consistency results were considered not significant when the 95% confidence intervals of inconsistency factors included zero or the RoR included one. 7. The certainty of evidence was not downgraded for indirectness because validated surrogate markers for ESKD were used. However, the lower end of the 95% confidence interval crossed the threshold of 10 per 1000 patients, suggesting there may be an important benefit. 8. The trials contributing more than 50% of the weight of the pooled estimate were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias in domains such as allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting. 9. The confidence interval crosses the line of no effect, suggesting that the difference could be importantly less or have no effect. The event rate was not available. 10. Two of the included trials, which contributed more than 30% of the weight of the pooled estimate, were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias in domains such as blinding of participants and personnel and selective reporting. 11. For the subgroup of patients with diabetic kidney disease, the certainty of evidence was rated as low. The lower end of the 95% confidence interval crossed the threshold of 10 per 1000 patients, suggesting there may be an important benefit. 12. The trial contributing most of the weight of the pooled estimate (over 80%) was judged to have an unclear risk of bias in blinding outcome assessment and selective reporting in another review. 13. The point estimates vary importantly with regard to the direction and magnitude of effect, and some of the confidence intervals do not overlap. There is high statistical heterogeneity, as reflected by the I-squared value of 82%. 14. The trial contributing most of the weight of the pooled estimate (LIFE trial, over 99%) was judged to have an unclear risk of bias for allocation concealment. 15. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low for adverse events, with an absolute effect of 15 more events per 1000 patients (ranging from 3 fewer to 45 more). Outcomes such as cognitive impairment/dementia and end-stage kidney disease were not reported. 16. The results are derived from a network meta-analysis that included one trial directly comparing ARB to placebo, three trials comparing ACE inhibitors to placebo, and two trials comparing ACE inhibitors to ARB, with a total of six trials in the network. 17. Included trials were judged to have an unclear risk of selection bias (random sequence generation, allocation concealment) and attrition bias. Adequate data to assess inconsistency and incoherence were not provided in the manuscript. Attempts to contact the authors for clarification or additional data were unsuccessful.
